question.text: Scenario: Lakshmi (age 55) works in the private sector and plans to retire in 5 years at age 60. Current monthly income: Rs. 2,00,000. Monthly expenses: Rs. 1,20,000. She saves Rs. 80,000 per month and will continue doing so until retirement. Existing corpus: Rs. 80,00,000 in EPF/PPF (expected return 7.5% p.a.), Rs. 40,00,000 in equity mutual funds (expected return 11% p.a.), Rs. 20,00,000 in Fixed Deposits (expected return 7.5% p.a.). NPS corpus expected to be Rs. 30,00,000 at age 60. No outstanding loans. No employer pension (private sector). Life expectancy: 85 years (25 years in retirement). Inflation: 6% p.a. Expected returns during retirement: debt 7.5% p.a., equity 11% p.a. Monthly savings of Rs. 80,000 are invested at a blended return of 10% p.a. NPS withdrawal rules: 60% lump sum (tax-free), 40% must purchase annuity at 6% p.a. yield. Question 5 of 5: As Lakshmi approaches retirement over the next 5 years, which asset allocation shift is most appropriate for her overall portfolio?

answer.text: Increase equity allocation to 70% to maximise growth in the final 5 years before retirement
Move 100% to fixed deposits and EPF for complete capital protection
Reduce equity exposure and increase allocation to debt and liquid retirement-income assets as retirement approaches
Maintain the current allocation unchanged since 5 years is still a medium-term horizon

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook states that as a goal nears funding, equity exposure should be reduced and the portfolio shifted toward safer, more liquid assets that match the spending profile of the goal. With only 5 years to retirement and a 25-year decumulation phase to follow, Lakshmi should gradually rotate from her current equity tilt toward short-term debt and liquid funds so that the corpus supporting early-retirement years is protected from sequence-of-returns risk. The Trap: Increasing equity to 70% exposes the corpus to severe sequence-of-returns risk just before retirement. 100% fixed-income sacrifices the inflation-beating equity exposure that the workbook says is still needed across a 25-year retirement. Maintaining status quo ignores the transition from the accumulation to the decumulation phase. Note: The workbook supports the direction of reducing equity and increasing debt/liquid assets as retirement nears, but does not prescribe an exact target ratio; any specific allocation percentage (for example 20-25% equity) should be treated as illustrative and tailored to the client's risk profile and income needs.
